Gross and operating margins were 63% and 33%, respectively, resulting in $231 million of operating income. During the quarter, we launched the CIRQA™ Smart Band, a screenless wearable offering rich wellness and fitness insights that expands our addressable market for wellness devices. In addition, we recently announced the next generation of Edge ® cycling computers with the Edge 1060 featuring a built-in microphone and speaker for hands-free voice control capability and the Edge Explore 3 series, an easy-to-use bike computer for riders of all levels. Outdoor: Revenue from the outdoor segment increased 20% in the third quarter with growth primarily driven by adventure watches. Gross and operating margins were 68% and 39%, respectively, resulting in $233 million of operating income. During the quarter, we launched the fēnix 9 and fēnix 9 Pro series, with an all-titanium watch case option and the largest available AMOLED screen in our flagship adventure watch lineup. Also during the quarter, we launched the all-new Garmin Drive TM GPS navigators with high-resolution ultrawide format displays and an elevated user experience. Aviation: Revenue from the aviation segment increased 5% in the third quarter with growth primarily driven by OEM product categories. Gross and operating margins were 78% and 26%, respectively, resulting in $66 million of operating income. During the quarter, we unveiled the G2000 ® PRIME, bringing PRIME flight deck functionality to the high-performance piston and electric aircraft market. Also during the quarter, we announced the certification of an all-glass retrofit cockpit for the original Cessna CitationJet. Pilatus Aircraft and Epic Aircraft recently announced the certification of Garmin Autoland on the PC-12 Pro and the e1000 airplanes, respectively. We also made important updates to Garmin Pilot™, adding SmartCharts coverage for Canada and Mexico, as well as Mobile Clearance Delivery which allows pilots to obtain clearances electronically through the Garmin Pilot app. Marine: Revenue from the marine segment increased 16% in the third quarter with broad-based growth across multiple categories, led by the sonar product category. Gross and operating margins were 64% and 30%, respectively, resulting in $94 million of operating income. During the quarter, we launched the next generation LiveScope TM 2, delivering live sonar images with improved range and clarity. Also during the quarter, we expanded our sailboat product lineup with the GMI TM 40 instrument display and the SmartDrive™ brushless linear steering actuator. We also launched the JL Audio A60 head unit series, and M200 speaker systems. Auto OEM: Revenue from the auto OEM segment decreased 20% during the third quarter primarily due to domain controllers.

excerpt: today announced its unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026. · Revenue: $281.2 million, up 0.6% year-over-year. · GAAP gross margin of 38.5%; non-GAAP gross margin of 42.1%, including benefit of approximately 200 basis points from IEEPA 1 refunds. · GAAP operating margin of -0.3%; non-GAAP operating margin of 5.0%. · Net cash used in operating activities of $24.5 million. · GAAP diluted loss per share of $0.10; non-GAAP diluted earnings per share of $0.09. · Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash of $71.7 million. The rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is reshaping network investment priorities, creating opportunities for ADTRAN not only in cloud infrastructure but also across our traditional service provider markets.” “Looking ahead, we see significant opportunities to build on this momentum as customers invest in network capacity, performance and security,” Stanton continued. “Our focus is on addressing the supply and cost pressures affecting our business, maintaining financial discipline and translating these opportunities into stronger revenue growth, profitability and cash generation.” Business outlook 1 For the fourth quarter of 2026, the Company expects revenue to be within a range of $272.0 million to $292.0 million. excerpt: 3Q26 Results (Comparisons are to year-ago periods unless indicated otherwise) Nightclubs segment: Revenues of $63.0 million increased by 1.0%. Four newly acquired, opened and reformatted clubs generated $4.0 million sales and the 52 clubs in same-store sales produced $58.5 million, more than offsetting $1.2 million in sales from four clubs closed subsequent to the year-ago quarter. 2 By revenue type, service increased 7.6%; food, merchandise and other declined 1.4%; and alcoholic beverages declined 4.2%. Impairments and other charges, net were immaterial compared to $2.3 million. Operating income was $19.6 million compared to $17.9 million or 31.2% of segment revenues compared to 28.6%. Probiotics for the prevention of Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea in adults and children.
Antibiotics can disturb gastrointestinal microbiota, which may lead to reduced resistance to pathogens such as Clostridioides difficile. Probiotics are live microbial preparations that, when administered in adequate amounts, may confer a health benefit to the host, and are a potential C difficile infection prevention strategy. To assess the benefits and harms of probiotics for preventing C difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) in adults and children receiving an antibiotic for any reason. We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, and Ovid Embase from 18 March 2017 (search date of the previous version of the review) to 3 March 2025. We included randomized controlled trials with a placebo, alternative prophylaxis, or no-treatment control investigating probiotics (any strain or dose) for the prevention of CDAD in adults and children receiving an antibiotic for any reason. The critical outcome was incidence of CDAD. Important outcomes included detection of C difficile in stool (i.e. colonization in absence of symptoms), adverse events, antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD), and length of hospital stay. Two review authors independently assessed risk of bias using Cochrane's RoB 1 tool. We pooled dichotomous outcomes (e.g. incidence of CDAD) using a random-effects complete-case model to calculate the risk ratio (RR) and absolute risk reduction (ARR) and corresponding 95% confidence interval (95% CI). We pooled continuous outcomes (e.g. length of hospital stay) using a random-effects model to calculate the mean difference (MD) and corresponding 95% CI. We conducted sensitivity analyses to explore the impact of missing outcome data on benefits and harms outcomes. To investigate heterogeneity, we conducted a priori subgroup analyses on risk of bias, probiotic dose, probiotic species, adults versus children, inpatients versus outpatients, and the event rate in the control group for developing CDAD (low 0% to 2%; moderate 3% to 5%; high > 5%). The certainty of the evidence for each outcome was independently assessed using the GRADE approach. Eight new studies (n = 4595) met our inclusion criteria, for a total of 47 included studies (n = 15,260). Although we noted a high risk of bias in individual studies for sequence generation or allocation concealment, this did not impact our findings. Around 30% of studies lacked a published protocol or clinical trial registration, and in some cases there were inconsistencies between the reported methods and published results. We noted authors' affiliation with a probiotic company and financial support received from probiotic companies in 28 studies. Evidence from 38 trials (13,179 participants) suggests that probiotics may result in a small absolute risk reduction (ARR) of 1.6% (incidence of 1.6% [110/6787] in the probiotic group versus 3.2% [203/6392] in the control group), and a relative risk reduction (RRR) of 50% (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.64; P < 0.001; low-certainty evidence) in incidence of CDAD. Twenty-seven of 38 trials had missing CDAD data, ranging from 2% to 45%. Our complete-case CDAD results proved robust to sensitivity analyses of plausible and worst-plausible assumptions regarding missing outcome data. Pooled results from 16 trials (1302 participants) suggest that probiotics may result in a small absolute reduction in C difficile in stool (i.e. colonization in absence of symptoms) (ARR 2.1%; incidence of 14.9% [101/677] in the probiotic group versus 16.2% [101/625] in the control group; RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.11; P = 0.27; low-certainty evidence). Thirty-seven studies (11,911 participants) reported on adverse events. Our pooled analysis indicates that probiotics probably result in a small ARR of 1.7% (incidence of 10.9% [669/6148] in the probiotic group versus 12.2% [701/5763] in the control group), and an RRR of 14.0% (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.01; P = 0.074; moderate-certainty evidence). The most common adverse events in both the treatment and control groups were abdominal cramping, nausea, fever, soft stools, flatulence, and taste disturbance. Pooled results from 40 studies (13,419 participants) suggest that probiotics may result in a large ARR of 9% (incidence of 23% [1592/6901] in the probiotic group versus 27.4% [1787/6518] in the control group), and an RRR of 33% (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.78; P < 0.001; low-certainty evidence) in incidence of AAD. Only seven trials (6553 participants) investigated length of hospital stay. There is likely little to no difference in length of hospital stay between treatment and control groups (MD -0.07, 95% CI -0.35 to 0.21; P = 0.63; moderate-certainty evidence). We downgraded the certainty of evidence for CDAD and AAD due to the low number of events or publication bias. We observed some variability in CDAD control group event rate (< 2% to > 5%) that may impact the applicability of evidence depending on clinical setting. We downgraded the certainty of evidence for adverse events due to variation between the results of the studies and for hospital stay due to selective reporting. The currently available evidence suggests that probiotics may be effective for preventing CDAD, suggesting that for every 65 people taking probiotics, one case of CDAD may be prevented (number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome of 65, 95% CI 48 to 97). There are probably fewer adverse events in the probiotic group. The short-term use of probiotics may have a small absolute benefit, and is likely not associated with adverse effects when used in patient populations receiving systemic antibiotics who are not immunocompromised. Large trials comparing probiotics with placebo in people with a low baseline risk of CDAD are needed. There was no source of funding for this update. The original review was done in 2013 by Johnston and colleagues, for which the protocol was developed. We followed the methods specified in the 2017 review, while modifying the search strategy and risk of bias assessment for selective reporting for this update.

excerpt:
Recurrence After Conjunctival Autograft versus Amniotic Membrane Transplantation for Primary Pterygium: A Retrospective Kaplan-Meier Cohort Study.
To compare recurrence after conjunctival autograft (CAG) and amniotic membrane transplantation (AMT) for primary pterygium and to identify unadjusted predictors of recurrence, with an exploratory analysis by age group. This retrospective cohort study included 402 patients who underwent primary pterygium excision by a single surgeon over 10 years (CAG, n=193; AMT, n=209). Patients chose their surgical technique after counselling, and all were followed for 12 months. The primary outcome was recurrence, defined as fibrovascular tissue extending ≥1.5 mm onto the cornea. Associations were assessed with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. All analyses were unadjusted; multivariable regression was not performed because of the limited number of recurrence events. Recurrence-free probability was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method and compared with the log-rank test. Effect sizes were reported as odds ratio (OR), absolute risk reduction (ARR), relative risk reduction (RRR), and number needed to treat (NNT). Age-stratified analyses were exploratory. The overall recurrence rate was 11.7% (47/402) at 12 months, and all recurrences occurred within 9 months. Recurrence was lower with CAG than AMT (8.3% vs 14.8%; Fisher's exact p=0.044), with an unadjusted OR for AMT of 1.93 (95% CI: 1.02-3.65), ARR of 6.5% points, RRR of 44.1%, and NNT of 15.3. Recurrence-free probability at 12 months was 91.7% with CAG and 85.2% with AMT (log-rank p=0.041). In exploratory age-stratified analyses, recurrence was 0% (0/54) with CAG vs 21.1% (15/71) with AMT in patients aged 20-40 years, with no difference in patients aged 41-60 years (11.1% vs 11.5%); the group aged >60 years (n=12) was too small to interpret. No other variable was associated with recurrence in unadjusted analyses. In this non-randomized cohort, in which patients chose their technique, CAG was associated with lower recurrence than AMT. The apparent difference in younger patients is hypothesis-generating only and requires prospective confirmation, and residual confounding, including by pterygium grade, cannot be excluded.

excerpt:
Effect of a Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Postoperative Sleep Disturbance After Oocyte Retrieval Under Intravenous Anesthesia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common complication after oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. This study aimed to evaluate whether a subanesthetic dose of esketamine reduces the incidence of PSD. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial included 196 women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Participants were randomly assigned to the esketamine or control group. During anesthesia induction, the esketamine group received an intravenous bolus of esketamine 0.2 mg/kg, whereas the control group received an equivalent volume of normal saline. The primary analysis was conducted according to the intention-to-treat principle, with missing outcome data handled using multiple imputation; 189 participants (95 in the control group and 94 in the esketamine group) were included in the per-protocol sensitivity analysis. The primary outcome was the incidence of PSD on postoperative day (POD) 3, defined using a composite criterion of an Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) score ≥6 or a numerical rating scale (NRS) score ≥6. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of PSD on POD 1, postoperative pain scores, postoperative anxiety and depression scores, and patient satisfaction with the anesthetic technique. In the intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation, the estimated incidence of PSD on POD 3 was lower in the esketamine group than in the control group (13.06% vs 24.90%; risk difference, -11.84 percentage points [95% CI, -22.98 to -0.69]; relative risk [RR], 0.52 [95% CI, 0.28-0.99]; P = 0.047). The per-protocol (PP) sensitivity analysis yielded similar results (12.8% vs 24.2%; RR, 0.53 [95% CI, 0.28-0.99]; P = 0.043). PSD on POD 1 did not differ between the groups. No between-group differences in postoperative anxiety or depression scores were noted. Postoperative pain scores at 30 minutes were significantly lower in the esketamine group (P < 0.001). Dreaming was more frequent in the esketamine group (21.4% vs 11.2%; P = 0.048), and the time to full alertness (12 [10-14] vs 11 [9-13] minutes; P = 0.002) and postanesthesia care unit (PACU) stay (34 [30-37] vs 31 [29-34] minutes; P = 0.005) were modestly longer. A single subanesthetic dose of esketamine was associated with a lower incidence of short-term PSD on POD 3 in women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Larger multicenter studies are warranted to confirm these findings. China Clinical Trial Registry Identifier: ChiCTR2500105998.
